Title: Regex Basics with 5 Real Examples
Desc: Learn the fundamentals of regular expressions (Regex) with practical examples that developers actually use for validation, searching, and text processing.
Author: MyWrite
Data:
## Regular Expressions, commonly called **Regex**, are one of the most powerful tools in programming.

They help you:

- Validate input
- Search text
- Extract data
- Replace content
- Automate text processing

At first glance, Regex looks confusing.

Example:

```regex
^[a-zA-Z0-9]+$
```

But once you understand the basics, it becomes much easier.

---

## What Is Regex?

Regex is a pattern used to match text.

Think of it as:

```text
Text
↓
Pattern
↓
Match Result
```

Instead of checking every character manually, you define rules.

---

## Why Developers Use Regex

Common use cases:

* Email validation
* Password validation
* URL matching
* Form processing
* Search functionality

Regex saves hundreds of lines of code in some situations.

---

## Basic Regex Symbols

### `.`

Matches any single character.

Example:

```regex
a.c
```

Matches:

```text
abc
axc
a1c
```

---

### `*`

Matches zero or more occurrences.

Example:

```regex
ab*
```

Matches:

```text
a
ab
abb
abbb
```

---

### `+`

Matches one or more occurrences.

Example:

```regex
ab+
```

Matches:

```text
ab
abb
abbb
```

But not:

```text
a
```

---

### `^`

Beginning of text.

Example:

```regex
^hello
```

Matches:

```text
hello world
```

But not:

```text
say hello
```

---

### `$`

End of text.

Example:

```regex
world$
```

Matches:

```text
hello world
```

## Example 1: Username Validation

Requirement:

```text
Only letters and numbers
```

Regex:

```regex
^[a-zA-Z0-9]+$
```

Matches:

```text
john123
User2026
```

Does not match:

```text
john_123
john@email
```

Useful for signup forms.

---

## Example 2: Email Validation

Basic regex:

```regex
^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$
```

Matches:

```text
user@example.com
hello@test.org
```

Does not match:

```text
user@
example.com
```

A common form validation use case.

---

## Example 3: Phone Number Validation

Requirement:

```text
Only 10 digits
```

Regex:

```regex
^\d{10}$
```

Matches:

```text
1234567890
```

Does not match:

```text
12345
12345678901
```

Useful for contact forms.

---

## Example 4: Find All Numbers

Regex:

```regex
\d+
```

Text:

```text
Order 123 costs 50 dollars
```

Matches:

```text
123
50
```

Perfect for extracting numeric values.

---

## Example 5: Validate URLs

Simple regex:

```regex
^https?:\/\/.+$
```

Matches:

```text
https://example.com
http://mysite.org
```

Does not match:

```text
example.com
ftp://server.com
```

Useful when validating links.

## Understanding Character Classes

### `[a-z]`

Lowercase letters.

---

### `[A-Z]`

Uppercase letters.

---

### `[0-9]`

Numbers.

---

### `[a-zA-Z]`

Any letter.

---

### `[a-zA-Z0-9]`

Letters and numbers.

---

## Useful Shortcuts

### `\d`

Digit.

Equivalent:

```regex
[0-9]
```

---

### `\w`

Word character.

Matches:

```text
Letters
Numbers
Underscores
```

---

### `\s`

Whitespace.

Matches:

```text
Space
Tab
Newline
```

---

## Quantifiers Explained

### `{3}`

Exactly 3 times.

Example:

```regex
\d{3}
```

---

### `{2,5}`

Between 2 and 5 times.

Example:

```regex
[a-z]{2,5}
```

---

### `{2,}`

At least 2 times.

---

## Regex in JavaScript

Example:

```js id="regex-js"
const regex = /^[a-zA-Z0-9]+$/;

console.log(regex.test("john123"));
```

Output:

```text
true
```

Simple validation with one line of code.

---

## Common Beginner Mistakes

### Making Regex Too Complex

Start simple.

---

### Forgetting `^` and `$`

These anchors control full-string matching.

---

### Using Regex for Everything

Sometimes plain string methods are easier.

---

### Not Testing Patterns

Always verify matches and edge cases.

---

## A Simple Regex Workflow

```text id="workflow"
Define Requirement
↓
Create Pattern
↓
Test Matches
↓
Test Invalid Cases
↓
Use In Application
```

## When Regex Is a Great Choice

Use Regex for:

* Validation
* Searching
* Data extraction
* Pattern matching

---

## When Regex Is Not Ideal

Avoid Regex for:

* Complex parsing
* Large structured data
* Tasks requiring business logic

Sometimes simpler code is better.

---

## FAQ

### What is Regex?

A pattern language used to match, search, and process text.

### Is Regex difficult to learn?

The basics are straightforward. Complexity comes with advanced patterns.

### Why do developers use Regex?

To validate, search, extract, and manipulate text efficiently.

### Is Regex fast?

For most common use cases, yes.

### Do all programming languages support Regex?

Most modern programming languages include Regex support.

---

## Final Thoughts

Regex may look intimidating at first, but its core idea is simple:

```text id="final-flow"
Pattern
↓
Match Text
↓
Perform Action
```

Start with basic validation and search patterns.

Over time, you'll discover that Regex is one of the most useful tools in a developer's toolkit—especially when working with forms, APIs, and text-heavy applications.
